newsitem.title: SYRIA: Syria welcomes first Iraqi trade visit in 17 years.
newsitem.headline: Syria welcomes first Iraqi trade visit in 17 years.

text.p: An Iraqi government and business delegation arrived in Syria on Friday for the first time in 17 years to a warm welcome from its Syrian hosts.

Officials and businessmen from both sides hugged each other before having lunch in an Arabian camel-wool tent installed especially to welcome the Iraqi team at a desert border outpost 300 km (185 miles) northeast of Damascus.
Syria's ties with Iraq were severed at the beginning of the 1980s after Damascus sided with Iran in its 1980-1988 war with Iraq.

The 37-strong Iraqi team, responding to a visit by Syrian businessmen to Baghdad last month, will have talks on importing Syrian commodities in line with Baghdad's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
Officials said the Iraqi team grouped the general directors of the ministries of industry, commerce and health.
Officials said the visit constituted the practical opening of the border for businessmen and traders announced by Syria earlier this month.
"Businessmen and traders of both countries can visit each other through arrangements by the chambers of commerce and industry in Syria and Iraq," one official said.
Several workers and technicians were busy on Friday fixing installations and stores on the Syrian side to prepare for the expected flow of trade.
Under a deal with the United Nations renewed earlier this month, Iraq can sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to pay for imports of basic needs.
Syria has been abiding by economic sanctions imposed on Iraq because of its invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
Rateb al-Shallah, head of Syria's chamber of commerce and industry, who visited Baghdad last month, told reporters that normal ties should be restored.
"...Whatever differences existed they should be forgotten. The normal relation which is natural should be resumed," Shallah said.
"Usually the resumption of ties in the economic field is followed, no matter how much later, by the resumption of other relations," he added.
Zuheir Abdul-Ghafour, head of Baghdad's chamber of commerce and industry who is leading the Iraqi team, said it was the hope of all Arabs to unite with each other.
"We came here to visit our brothers and our visit is not strange," he said.
Diplomats said some time was still needed before a decision on resuming diplomatic relations could be made by Syria.

Asked about the quota which Syria could get as part of Iraq's new deal with the U.N., Ghafour said: "We wish to give Syria the biggest share, but this issue is linked to the kind of offers, prices, and the approval of the U.N."
Officials said the Syrian and Iraqi delegations would resume talks on the reopening of an Iraqi pipeline that used to carry oil to the Mediterranean through Syria but was closed in 1982.
